title: First Battle of the Marne
summary: Seven days on the Ourcq, the two Morins and the marshes of Saint-Gond. Maunoury's 6th Army finds Kluck's open flank north-east of Meaux on 5 September; Kluck swings four corps back across the Marne to meet it and wins on the Ourcq, but every corps he moves widens the gap between his army and Bülow's, into which the BEF and Franchet d'Espèrey's 5th Army advance. Foch holds the marshes against Bülow's left and Hausen's night attack. On the evening of 8 September Moltke's emissary Hentsch reaches Bülow; on the morning of the 9th, with the British across the Marne, Bülow retreats and Hentsch tells Kluck to conform. The right wing marches for the Aisne.
outcome: German 1st and 2nd Armies retreat to the Aisne from 9 September; the Schlieffen timetable is dead and the mobile war in the West ends within the month.

events.title: Gronau meets Maunoury: the Ourcq opens
events.summary: North-east of Meaux, around Monthyon and Saint-Soupplets, the IV Reserve Corps — Kluck's flank guard — runs into the 55th and 56th Reserve Divisions leading Maunoury's advance out of Paris. Gronau attacks, then falls back in the night; Kluck learns that his open flank has been found.

events.title: Kluck recalls the II Corps across the Marne
events.summary: From his headquarters Kluck orders the II Corps back north over the Marne to the Ourcq — the first of four corps he will swing away from the BEF and the French 5th Army over the next three days.

events.title: Joffre's order of the day: the hour has come
events.summary: The general counter-offensive begins. Joffre's order of the day tells the armies that the battle on which the safety of the country depends has begun, that every effort must go to attacking and throwing back the enemy, and that troops which can no longer advance must hold the ground won at any price and be killed on the spot rather than fall back.

events.title: The BEF and the French 5th Army turn about
events.summary: After a fortnight's retreat the British and Franchet d'Espèrey's army face north again. The BEF advances from the Tournan–Rozay line towards the Grand Morin; the 5th Army attacks Kluck's III and IX Corps at Esternay — the corps Kluck is about to pull away to the Ourcq.

events.title: The taxis of the Marne leave Paris
events.summary: On Gallieni's order some 600 Paris taxis, requisitioned that afternoon, carry part of the 7th Division from Gagny and Livry to Nanteuil-le-Haudouin and Silly-le-Long in two runs through the night — four to five thousand men, a fraction of Maunoury's reinforcements, and the most famous image of the battle.

events.title: Hausen's night attack at Fère-Champenoise
events.summary: At three in the morning the Saxon XII Corps and the Guard go forward with the bayonet, without artillery preparation, against Foch's right at the eastern end of the marshes of Saint-Gond. The IX and XI Corps are driven back several kilometres and Fère-Champenoise is lost — the last German success of the battle.

events.title: Hentsch at Bülow's headquarters, Montmort
events.summary: Having visited the 5th, 4th and 3rd Army headquarters, Hentsch reaches Bülow at Montmort in the evening. Bülow and his staff judge the 2nd Army's position untenable once the BEF crosses the Marne into the gap; the two agree that if it does, the 2nd Army will retreat and the 1st must conform.

events.title: The BEF crosses the Marne
events.summary: The I and II Corps cross at Charly and Nanteuil-sur-Marne in the morning; at La Ferté-sous-Jouarre the bridges are down and the III Corps needs until the next day. German airmen report the British columns north of the river — the report that decides Bülow.

events.title: Bülow orders the 2nd Army to retreat
events.summary: With the British across the Marne on his open right, Bülow orders his army back behind the Marne towards Dormans and Épernay, and tells OHL and Kluck.

events.title: Hentsch at Kluck's headquarters, Mareuil: the 1st Army is to retreat
events.summary: Hentsch reaches Mareuil-sur-Ourcq late in the morning, after a drive through the retreating columns of the 2nd Army's right, and tells Kluck's chief of staff, Kuhl, that the 2nd Army is retreating and the 1st must fall back to the Aisne. Kluck, who believes he is winning on the Ourcq, obeys. Whether Hentsch had the authority — Vollmacht — to order it, and whether the battle was already lost, is the oldest dispute about the Marne.

events.title: The right wing stands on the Aisne
events.summary: After three days of pursuit the 1st and 2nd Armies are across the Aisne between Compiègne and Reims; when the Allies arrive on 13 September the Germans are dug in on the heights north of the river and the war of movement ends.

title: Liège
summary: Twelve Brialmont forts in a ring around the Meuse crossings, the first obstacle on the right wing's road. Emmich's six brigades try to rush the intervals on the night of 5/6 August and fail; Ludendorff, taking over a brigade whose commander has been killed, reaches the heights and bluffs the citadel into surrender on the 7th; Leman sends his field division away and fights on from the forts. They fall one by one from 8 August — Barchon first — and in a rush from the 12th, when the 42 cm and 30.5 cm howitzers arrive; Loncin explodes on the 15th with Leman inside; Hollogne and Flémalle give up on the 16th. Whether the defence cost the timetable anything is argued.
outcome: The city taken on 7 August, the forts by 16 August; the 1st and 2nd Armies march from the 18th. Leman a prisoner; the heavy howitzers' reputation made.

formations.name: Army of the Meuse (Emmich)
formations.summary: Six reinforced brigades drawn from the 2nd Army's corps (the 11th, 14th, 27th, 34th, 38th and 43rd) under Otto von Emmich, formed for the coup de main on Liège; Ludendorff rode with it as OHL's liaison. About 39,000 men and 124 guns.

formations.name: 14th Infantry Brigade
formations.summary: Wussow's brigade, which Ludendorff took over when its commander was killed on the morning of 6 August; it was the only one of the six to break through the intervals, reached the heights above the city and took the citadel on 7 August.

formations.name: 27th Infantry Brigade
formations.summary: Attacked between Barchon and Évegnée on the night of 5/6 August and was thrown back.

formations.name: 34th Infantry Brigade
formations.summary: Crossed the Meuse at Lixhe on the north of the ring and attacked between Pontisse and Liers; repulsed with heavy loss at Rabosée.

formations.name: 11th Infantry Brigade
formations.summary: Attacked between Fléron and Chaudfontaine; repulsed on 6 August.

formations.name: 38th and 43rd Infantry Brigades
formations.summary: The southern attack over the Ourthe between Embourg and Boncelles; thrown back on the night of 5/6 August.

concentration.area: Essen → Aachen by rail, then by road

formations.summary: Two of Krupp's 42 cm M-Gerät howitzers, brought by road from Aachen when the railway was blocked, in action against Pontisse from the evening of 12 August and then against the western forts from inside the city.

formations.name: 30.5 cm mortar batteries (Škoda)
formations.summary: Austro-Hungarian 30.5 cm Škoda mortars lent to the German army, in action against the eastern forts from 12–13 August.

formations.name: Leman's headquarters
formations.summary: Leman's headquarters in the Rue Sainte-Foi in Liège until the morning of 6 August, when a German patrol reached it and he withdrew to Fort Loncin to direct the forts; taken unconscious from Loncin's ruins on 15 August.

The division held the intervals on the night of 5/6 August and was sent back to the field army on the Gette by Leman on the 6th.
Marwitz's cavalry crossed the Meuse at Lixhe on 4 August and screened north of the ring towards Tongeren and Sint-Truiden; Haelen on 12 August.

events.title: German troops cross the Belgian frontier at Gemmenich
events.summary: Belgium having refused passage on 3 August, Emmich's Army of the Meuse and Marwitz's cavalry cross the frontier near Gemmenich and Aachen on the morning of 4 August and close on the Meuse.

events.title: Emmich's demand refused; the bombardment begins
events.summary: A parlementaire's demand for free passage is refused by Leman; German field guns open on the eastern forts and Zeppelin L Z VI bombs the city on the night of 5/6 August.

events.title: The night assault on the intervals
events.summary: Five brigades attack the gaps between the forts in the dark and are thrown back with heavy loss — Rabosée, Retinne, the Ourthe; only the 14th Brigade, its commander Wussow killed and Ludendorff in his place, gets through to the heights above the city.

events.title: Leman sends the 3rd Division away
events.summary: With a German brigade on the heights and the intervals no longer tenable, Leman orders the 3rd Division back to the field army on the Gette and moves his own headquarters into Fort Loncin. The forts will fight on alone.

events.title: Ludendorff takes the citadel
events.summary: Ludendorff drives into the city with his brigade adjutant, hammers on the citadel gate and receives the surrender of its garrison; the city is German, the forts are not.

events.title: Fort de Barchon surrenders — the first
events.summary: Barchon, battered by 21 cm mortars and cut off, is the first of the twelve to give up.

events.title: The first 42 cm shell falls on Pontisse
events.summary: Krupp's M-Gerät, brought by road from Aachen, opens fire from Mortier; Pontisse is wrecked and surrenders the next day. The fortress, the strongest of its type in Europe, has met the weapon built to break it.

events.title: Pontisse, Embourg and Chaudfontaine fall
events.summary: Three forts in a day under the 42 cm and 30.5 cm howitzers; at Chaudfontaine the magazine explodes.

events.title: Fort de Loncin explodes; Leman taken
events.summary: A 42 cm shell reaches Loncin's magazine; the fort blows up with most of its garrison, and Leman is dug unconscious from the ruins and taken prisoner.

events.title: Visé burned
events.summary: The town of Visé on the Meuse, where the cavalry had crossed on 4 August, is sacked and burned by German troops on 15–16 August and some 600 of its people deported — one of the August massacres and burnings that Horne and Kramer trace to the franc-tireur panic.

events.title: Hollogne and Flémalle surrender — the last forts
events.summary: The last two forts on the left bank give up on the morning of 16 August; the road and railway through Liège are open, and the 1st and 2nd Armies begin their march on the 18th.
